chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn al-Hamid from Abu Jamilah from al-Hasan ibn Ziyad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

When a man has intercourse with a woman and she then claims the dowry while he says, 'I have given it to you,' the burden of proof is upon her and the oath is upon him. And if the matter were according to what some of our companions believed—that if he had intercourse with her, it would invalidate the dowry—there would be no burden of proof upon her and no oath upon him, because intercourse has already removed the right, so there is no basis for establishing proof or an oath. It is also possible that the reason in those narrations is that if he did not specify a definite dowry but gave her something, that becomes her dowry and she has nothing else after that. And in none of them is it stated that he used to specify a definite dowry. What indicates this is what al-Fudayl ibn Yasar narrated in the preceding report from his saying: 'That which you took before he had intercourse with her is that which made her private part lawful to him, and she has nothing else after that.' This points to what we said, that he did not stipulate a definite dowry for her.
ai.seo_question: What is the burden of proof when a husband claims he paid the dowry after marital relations?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi presents this hadith in *al-Istibsar* to clarify the evidentiary burden in marital financial disputes, specifically addressing the scenario where a husband claims payment of the dowry after consummation. The text contrasts the dominant view that the wife must prove non-payment with an alternative interpretation where unspecified gifts constitute the full dowry, thereby extinguishing further claims. This reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on distinguishing between named dowries and general gifts to prevent unjust enrichment.
